summary: Describes how Novell IPX operates over various WAN media, including the IPX WAN protocol used for exchanging router information before normal routing starts. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before two far-apart routers start working together, they first introduce themselves. This describes that handshake.

questions: how does ipx work over wan links
how are master and slave chosen in ipxwan
subtitle: The introduction two Novell IPX routers exchange over a WAN link before normal routing starts.

tldr.problem: IPX is a connectionless datagram protocol, but WAN links are often connection-oriented and differ from one medium to another, so routers need a common way to start using a link.
tldr.mechanism: After the link is up, the two ends exchange Timer Request and Timer Response packets to pick a master and a routing type and to measure link delay, then the master sends an Information Request to set the final link configuration.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives one common IPX WAN protocol for PPP, X.25 and Frame Relay. It obsoletes RFC 1362 and RFC 1551 and is informational, not a standard.

today: RFC 1634 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 1362 and RFC 1551. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Running IPX over WAN Media
sections.content:
This document describes how Novell IPX operates over various wide area network (WAN) media. It is motivated by a wish for IPX to treat all wide area links in the same manner. Sections 3 and 4 describe the common IPX WAN (IPXWAN) protocol, which begins immediately after link establishment.

What "link establishment" means depends on the medium. With PPP, it means the IPX control protocol (IPXCP) reaches the Open state, and IPXWAN MUST NOT start before that. With X.25 switched virtual circuits it means opening a virtual circuit, which carries the protocol identifier 0x800000008137 in the Call User Data field. With X.25 permanent circuits no call is made, so the link counts as established when X.25 Layer 2 is up. With Frame Relay it means a permanent virtual circuit changing from inactive to active.

In each case IPX packets are carried without additional framing, and when a router sees the link go down it updates its routing information at once instead of waiting for entries to age out.
sections.eli5: Different kinds of long-distance cables have different ways of saying the line is ready. IPXWAN waits for that signal and then starts its own hello.

sections.title: Choosing Master, Slave and Routing Type
sections.content:
Both ends send Timer Request packets every 20 seconds until a response arrives or the sender decides the remote node is not responding (after a predefined time of at least 60 seconds, or a number of retries such as 16). Each request lists the routing types the sender supports, most preferred first.

The roles come from the WNodeID field. If both are zero, the router offering an Extended Node ID option with the higher value is master. Otherwise the higher nonzero WNodeID wins. Equal values are a configuration error and the link is disconnected. The master role carries no special privileges: it only means being the requestor in the following exchanges. Comparisons treat the first byte as most significant.

The slave answers with a Timer Response, accepting the first routing type it supports and setting WAccept to NO on all the others. If it supports none, it MUST disconnect. A router MUST NOT accept workstation connectivity to a node that is another router.
sections.eli5: Both sides shout their phone numbers. The one with the bigger number gets to ask the questions, but that does not make them the boss.

sections.title: IPXWAN Packet Formats
sections.content:
All IPXWAN exchanges use the standard IPX packet format with IPX packet type 04 and the reserved socket 0x9004. Network number zero means a local network of unknown number, which lets packets flow before a common network number is agreed. Each packet carries the identifier 57 41 53 4D in the WIdentifier field, and packets without it on that socket should be discarded.

The four packet types are Timer Request (00), Timer Response (01), Information Request (02) and Information Response (03). A NAK (FFh) is an exact copy of a received packet with the type changed, returned when the type is not recognized or the packet is badly formed. Timer packets are always 576 bytes, filled out with a PAD option of random data so that compressing modems cannot distort the delay measurement.

The Timer Request options include the Routing Type (option 00), Extended Node ID (04), Header Compression (80) and PAD (FF). Only one header compression option may be accepted.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with the same secret password bytes, so the receiver knows it is a real IPXWAN note and not random noise.

sections.title: The Information Exchange
sections.content:
Once roles and routing type are settled, the master sends an Information Request to the slave. It carries the link delay, the common network number, and the 48-character Router Name. For workstations a second option carries the NIC address. For Unnumbered RIP and on-demand links the network number is zero. The slave echoes the values in an Information Response.

The master measures link delay from the time between sending a Timer Request and receiving the Timer Response. The RFC gives code that uses units of 1/18th second, multiplies by 6 to bias for multiple sessions, and multiplies by 55 to get milliseconds. The delay then serves as the transport time advertised in IPX RIP for the common network.

For Unnumbered RIP, on-demand and workstation links, Information Requests repeat every 20 seconds until answered, each with an incremented sequence number. Numbered RIP links do not resend the request; they disconnect after a suitable delay of at least 60 seconds.
sections.eli5: The leader times how long a message takes to travel and then tells both sides the final settings, like which name tag each one wears.

sections.title: Routing Types and Workstations
sections.content:
The current routing types are 00 Numbered RIP/SAP, 01 NLSP, 02 Unnumbered RIP/SAP, 03 On Demand with static routing, and 04 Workstation. NLSP is not described in this RFC.

Unnumbered RIP runs RIP and SAP across a link with no IPX network number, so no pool of WAN network numbers has to be configured and fewer routing updates flood the network. On-demand, static routing means a router connects only when it has data to send, sends no RIP, SAP or NLSP, and uses configured routes and services identified by a Remote System Identifier. For PPP links, Novell uses PAP or CHAP to identify the caller.

A workstation connecting for the first time sets WNodeID to zero so the router becomes master and assigns a network number. A reconnecting workstation sets it to FFFFFFFFh to become master and keep its old address. Workstations need no periodic RIP and SAP broadcasts, so routers send RIP and SAP to them only on request.
sections.eli5: Some links can skip handing out street names, and some only dial when there is something to send. Home computers get just the news they ask for.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC states only that security issues are not discussed in the memo. For on-demand static routing it notes that the called router must identify the caller, and that PPP authentication can be used for this, but it defines no security mechanism of its own.
sections.eli5: The RFC does not talk about locks and keys. It only mentions that a router has to know who is calling.
